Architecture

The service has three layers. Each has one responsibility and a narrow interface to the next, which is what makes the layers testable in isolation.

┌───────────────────────────── Web layer ─────────────────────────────┐
│ flask_app.py   create_app()  GET /analysis  POST /pull-data          │
│                BusyState     POST /update-analysis  GET /status      │
└──────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────┘
               │ reads (ORM)                      │ triggers
┌──────────────▼───────────┐          ┌──────────▼──────────────────────┐
│ Query layer              │          │ ETL layer                        │
│ orm_queries.py (SQLAlchemy)         │ pull_new_data.py  (orchestrates) │
│ query_data.py  (raw SQL)  │          │ scrape.py → clean.py →           │
│ models.py      (Applicant)│          │ standardize.py → load_data.py    │
└──────────────┬───────────┘          └──────────┬──────────────────────┘
               │                                  │ psycopg
┌──────────────▼──────────────────────────────────▼──────────────────────┐
│ Database layer – PostgreSQL, table ``applicants`` (p_id primary key)   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Web layer (Flask)

flask_app.create_app(...) builds the application. Everything the routes need is injected: the database URL, a scrape function, a standardize function, a query function and a flask_app.BusyState. Production uses the real collaborators; tests pass fakes.

  • GET /analysis (and /) renders templates/index.html. Every number on the page comes from orm_queries.gather_results(), i.e. through the SQLAlchemy Applicant model; the routes never write SQL themselves.

  • POST /pull-data acquires the busy flag, runs pull_new_data.pull() (in a background thread in production, inline in tests) and answers JSON. A second request while busy gets 409 {"busy": true}.

  • POST /update-analysis re-queries the database and answers 200 {"ok": true}; while a pull is running it answers 409 {"busy": true} and does nothing else. It never starts a scrape.

  • GET /status reports the busy flag and the last pull’s outcome; the page polls it while a pull runs.

The buttons carry stable selectors, data-testid="pull-data-btn" and data-testid="update-analysis-btn", and every analysis item is labelled Answer:.

ETL layer

pull_new_data orchestrates one pull:

  1. read the entry URLs already stored (pull_new_data.known_urls());

  2. scrape.GradCafeScraper.scrape_new_entries() walks the listing from the newest page, following the cursor “Next” link, and stops at the first page that yields no unseen entry;

  3. clean.clean_data() strips HTML, normalizes status/degree and turns badge text such as GPA 3.85 into bare values;

  4. clean.standardize_rules_only() (or clean.standardize_with_llm()) fills llm-generated-program / llm-generated-university using the canonical lists in llm_hosting/;

  5. load_data.load_records() inserts with ON CONFLICT (p_id) DO NOTHING.

Everything is committed at the end of the pipeline, so a failure anywhere leaves the table unchanged.

Database layer

One table, applicants, exactly as specified in Module 3:

p_id integer PRIMARY KEY, program text, comments text, date_added date,
url text UNIQUE, status text, term text, us_or_international text,
gpa float, gre float, gre_v float, gre_aw float, degree text,
llm_generated_program text, llm_generated_university text

p_id is the numeric id at the end of each Grad Cafe entry URL (/result/1020478 → 1020478). It is stable across scrapes, which is what makes loading idempotent. models maps the same table for SQLAlchemy; load_data owns the schema (CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS).

Query layer

query_data answers the eleven analysis questions in raw SQL through psycopg; orm_queries answers them with SQLAlchemy select() / func expressions and provides orm_queries.gather_results(), the dictionary the template renders. Both apply the same rules: case-insensitive matching, percentages as 100.0 * COUNT(...) FILTER / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0) rounded to two decimals, and a metric counts as “provided” only when the value is possible on its scale (GRE 130–170, GRE AW 0–6, GPA 0–4.0).
